query: For high-entropy alloys intended for thermal-insulation or radiation-resistant applications, what single intervention could reduce phonon thermal conductivity? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention, the physical mechanism, the predicted change relative to an otherwise comparable untreated alloy, the temperature and material-state boundaries over which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing lattice distortions through alloying elements with different atomic radii can reduce phonon thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy with a simple unit cell
generation.intervention: Alloying with elements of different atomic radii
generation.mechanism: Scattering of phonons by lattice distortions
generation.baseline: Untreated high-entropy alloy with no lattice distortions
generation.boundary: Temperature range: 800°C to 1200°C, material state: solid solution phase
generation.uncertainty: The exact relationship between lattice distortions and phonon thermal conductivity is not well understood and requires further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Measure phonon thermal conductivity of high-entropy alloys with varying levels of lattice distortions introduced through alloying elements with different atomic radii.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no correlation is found between lattice distortions and phonon thermal conductivity, the hypothesis is falsified.

Superconductivity in a uranium containing high entropy alloy

Abstract: High entropy alloys (HEA) are an unusual class of materials where mixtures of elements are stochastically arrayed on a simple crystalline lattice. These systems exhibit remarkable functionality, often along several distinct axes: e.g., the examples [TaNb]1-x(TiZrHf)x are high strength and damage resistant refractory metals that also exhibit superconductivity with large upper critical fields. Here we report the discovery of an f-electron containing HEA, [TaNb]0.31(TiUHf)0.69, which is the first to include an actinide ion. Similar to the Zr-analogue, this material crystallizes in a body-centered cubic lattice with the lattice constant a = 3.41(1) Å and exhibits phonon mediated superconductivity with a transition temperatures Tc ≈ 3.2 K and upper critical fields Hc2 ≈ 6.4 T. These results expand this class of materials to include actinide elements, shows that superconductivity is robust in this sub-group, and opens the path towards leveraging HEAs as functional waste forms for a variety of radioisotopes.

Phonon behavior in a random solid solution: a lattice dynamics study on the high-entropy alloy FeCoCrMnNi

Abstract: AbstractHigh-Entropy Alloys (HEAs) are a new family of crystalline random alloys with four or more elements in a simple unit cell, at the forefront of materials research for their exceptional mechanical properties. Their strong chemical disorder leads to mass and force-constant fluctuations which are expected to strongly reduce phonon lifetime, responsible for thermal transport, similarly to glasses. Still, the long range order would associate HEAs to crystals with a complex disordered unit cell. These two families of materials, however, exhibit very different phonon dynamics, still leading to similar thermal properties. The question arises on the positioning of HEAs in this context. Here we present an exhaustive experimental investigation of the lattice dynamics in a HEA, Fe20Co20Cr20Mn20Ni20, using inelastic neutron and X-ray scattering. We demonstrate that HEAs present unique phonon dynamics at the frontier between fully disordered and ordered materials, characterized by long-propagating acoustic phonons in the whole Brillouin zone.Subject terms: Electronic proper
